title: File:Video of a pod of three striped dolphins (Stenella coeruleoalba) and echolocation clicks recorded by an underwater Spydro camera attached on a branchline of a pelagic longline deployed in the Eastern Corsica (Ifremer 00949-106047).webm

title: File:Seagrass Meadow - Porthdinllaen.webm
artist: Natural Resources Wales / Cyfoeth Naturiol Cymru
desc:
This video published by Natural Resources Wales / Cyfoeth Naturiol Cymru.
Published on 3 May 2017.
Text:
This seagrass meadow is a haven for marine life.
The baited underwater camera attracted a large Bull Huss and Conger eel.
Seagrass meadows are important for juvenile fish such as cod, plaice, herring and pollack.
They also help mitigate climate change by trapping vast amounts of carbon dioxide.
A large Bull Huss also stopped by.

Find out more: www.penllynarsarnau.co.uk and www.projectseagrass.org

title: File:Seafloor bathymetry and biodiversity of Arafura Marine Park.webm
desc: This flythrough highlights seabed environments within two areas of Arafura Marine Park offshore northern Australia; Money Shoal and Pillar Bank. Money Shoal is an isolated carbonate reef platform that rises from 70 m to shallow subtidal depths and supports a diverse coral and demersal fish community. desc: A segment of an event, which resulted in cleaning interactions being interrupted by another thresher shark. title: File:Oreaster reticulatus (reticulated starfish) (San Salvador Island, Bahamas) 8.webm
desc:
Oreaster reticulatus (Linnaeus, 1758) - reticulated starfish on shallow subtidal estuarine seafloor.
Most starfish are distinctively pentaradial, with five arms.  Numerous tube feet occur in the ambulacral grooves running down the axis of each arm's underside.  Many starfish are predatory and consume prey by everting their stomachs through their mouths (center structure on underside) and digest food externally.  Oreaster reticulatus is predatory on a variety of invertebrates and is also a deposit feeder.

desc: From Feb. 17, 2021, NOAA satellites monitored a large plume of dust from the Sahara Desert as it traveled off the west coast of North Africa and across the Atlantic Ocean. The geostationary GOES-16 (GOES East) satellite keeps constant vigil over the same area, orbiting more than 22,300 miles above the equator, at the same speed the Earth rotates. This view allows us to see the dust in motion. The polar-orbiting NOAA-20 satellite captured a dramatic image of dust particles blowing out over the Atlantic on Feb. 18.
